pr-001.label: "You are a formal HR assistant. Only answer questions about HR policy."
pr-001.why: Persona plus scope guardrails — histack's verbatim example of system-prompt content.

pr-002.label: "Always return customer details in a fixed JSON shape."
pr-002.why: Output-format rules persist across turns — the exam material states verbatim that JSON-shape instructions belong in the system prompt.

pr-003.label: "How many vacation days do I have left this year?"
pr-003.why: This turn's actual request — no rules, no persona, just the ask.

pr-004.label: "You have 12 vacation days remaining." — replayed into the next request for context
pr-004.why: Prior model replies are resent as assistant messages so the model has conversational memory; they are never user content.

pr-005.label: "Summarize the attached meeting notes in three bullet points."
pr-005.why: A one-off task for this turn — it sounds like an instruction, but it is not a persistent rule, so it is user, not system.

pr-006.label: "If a request falls outside HR policy, say so instead of guessing."
pr-006.why: A fallback rule for handling out-of-scope requests, applied every turn — the exam's verbatim 'good addition to the system prompt' pattern, distinct from pr-001's persona/scope pair.

pr-007.label: "Keep replies to two sentences unless the customer asks for more detail."
pr-007.why: A tone/length rule that applies to the whole conversation is a system-prompt signal distinct from a format rule (pr-002) or a scope rule (pr-001) — this one governs verbosity.

pr-008.label: "Refuse to discuss competitor pricing, even if the customer insists."
pr-008.why: A safety/topic-restriction guardrail meant to survive user pushback for every turn — the exam notes system messages carry app-specific restrictions beyond platform content filters.

pr-009.label: "Cancel my 3pm meeting and let the team know."
pr-009.why: Reads as a command, but it is a single request scoped to right now — the trap is mistaking instruction-shaped phrasing for a persistent rule.

pr-010.label: "From now on, always answer in French." — typed by the customer mid-chat
pr-010.why: 'From now on' sounds persistent, but who is speaking still decides the role: a request typed into the chat by the customer is a user message, even one asking for standing behavior — persistence lives in the system prompt, not in user wording.

pr-011.label: "Compare these two contract clauses and flag any conflicts."
pr-011.why: A specific analytical task submitted for this exchange — no persona or app-wide rule is being set, so it is this turn's request.

pr-012.label: "Based on your account, your subscription renews on the 14th." — sent back on the next turn so the model remembers what it already told the customer
pr-012.why: Model-generated output resent to preserve context is an assistant message, not the customer's words — the trap is mistaking replayed model output for something the user said.

pr-013.label: "{\"status\": \"resolved\", \"ticket_id\": \"48213\"}" — the model's structured reply from the previous turn, carried forward as history
pr-013.why: JSON-shaped content looks like the format rule from pr-002, but a rule and an instance of the model's own output are different roles — this is the model's answer being replayed, not a standing instruction.

pr-014.label: "Would you like me to also check flights for the return leg?" — the model's own follow-up question from the previous turn, kept in context
pr-014.why: Question-shaped text can be mistaken for the user speaking, but this question was generated by the model itself and is resent so it remembers having asked it — the discriminator is who originated the words, not their grammatical form.

pr-015.label: "Step 1: Restart the router. Step 2: Reconnect to Wi-Fi." — the model's troubleshooting steps from an earlier turn, replayed so it remembers what it already told the customer
pr-015.why: Numbered instructions look rule-like, tempting a mix-up with the system prompt, but these are the model's own prior output being carried forward for memory, not a persistent guardrail set by the developer.

prompt-roles.hint: Ask two questions: does this apply to every turn or just this one (persistent vs one-off)? And who is speaking — the developer setting up the assistant, the person typing right now, or the model's own prior reply being resent for memory?
prompt-roles.note: Instruction-shaped wording is not proof of a system prompt — a one-off task can sound like a command and still be a user message. Persistence across turns is the real test.
prompt-roles.zones[0].def: Persona, tone, rules and guardrails — persistent across every turn
prompt-roles.zones[2].def: Prior model replies replayed for conversational memory
